facts.statehood_note: Utah was a U.S. territory from 1850. It was admitted as the 45th state after it agreed to outlaw polygamy in its state constitution.
borders: New Mexico (touches only at the Four Corners)

symbols.name: Quaking aspen (2014, replacing the blue spruce)

facts.name_origin: Utah is named for the Ute people. The name comes from the Spanish word "Yuta," and is commonly said to mean "people of the mountains."

government.chambers: Utah Senate (29 members, 4-year terms) and Utah House of Representatives (75 members, 2-year terms). The Legislature meets every year for 45 days, starting in January.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term) and Lieutenant Governor (4-year term). Voters also elect an Attorney General, State Auditor, and State Treasurer, each for 4 years.
government.courts: Utah Supreme Court (5 justices, appointed by the Governor) is the highest court; below it are the Utah Court of Appeals and district courts in 8 judicial districts.
government.local: 29 counties, with Salt Lake County the largest. Utah's eight federally recognized tribal nations have their own governments.
government.constitution: Written at the Utah Constitutional Convention of 1895 and in force since statehood on January 4, 1896. It outlawed polygamy, as Congress required, and it gave women equal voting rights.
government.kid_line: "Both male and female citizens of this State shall enjoy equally all civil, political and religious rights and privileges." (Utah Constitution, Article IV, Section 1)

long_ago.about: People first came to the land that is now Utah about 12,000 years ago. Archaic people, about 8,000 years ago, lived by hunting and gathering and had to search carefully for food and water.

From about AD 1 to 1300, Fremont people lived in much of Utah. They hunted, gathered, and grew corn, lived in small villages of pit houses, wore moccasins, made gray pottery and baskets, and carved rock art in places like Nine Mile Canyon.

From about 300 BC to AD 1300, Ancestral Puebloan people lived in the red rock canyon country of southern Utah. They grew corn, beans, and squash, built pithouses and later stone buildings several stories high, and gathered in kivas for ceremonies.

The Ute moved to deserts and valleys in winter and to the mountains in summer. After horses arrived in the 1600s, they became noted hunters who traveled widely, and Spanish New Mexico began trading with them in the 1750s.
The Goshute were skilled hunters and gatherers in the desert southwest of the Great Salt Lake. They used more than 80 wild plants and roots, plus crickets, grasshoppers, and pinyon nuts.

Paiute people moved with the seasons and also farmed corn; Shoshone people traveled on foot across the Great Basin and used tipis; desert peoples built wickiups and hogans, and the Diné are known for their rich oral storytelling tradition.

today.nation: Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation
today.about: Formed in 1934 by the Uintah, White River, and Uncompahgre bands; its lands are in the Uinta Basin east of Salt Lake City.
A Weeminuche Ute nation in the Four Corners region; its White Mesa community is 11 miles south of Blanding.
A confederation of five bands (Cedar, Indian Peaks, Kanosh, Koosharem, and Shivwits) on land in four southwestern Utah counties.
Federally recognized in 1989; its Utah members live around Navajo Mountain, White Mesa, and Blanding.

today.nation: Confederated Tribes of the Goshute Reservation
today.about: Its Deep Creek Reservation straddles the Utah-Nevada border about 60 miles south of Wendover.
A Goshute nation with a reservation in Tooele County, about 90 miles west of Salt Lake City.

today.nation: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation
today.about: A Shoshone nation whose homeland is in northern Utah and southern Idaho.
The Diné homeland, Diné Bikéyah, reaches into southeastern Utah; its capital is Window Rock, Arizona.

first_peoples.today_note: Utah has eight federally recognized tribal nations, and about 60,000 Native Americans from more than 50 tribal nations live in Utah today. In 1861 President Lincoln set aside the Uintah Valley reservation for Ute people, after settlers rejected the land as poor; later allotments (1897 and 1904) cut Ute lands from nearly four million acres to 360,000 acres.
sites: Fremont Indian State Park, Clear Creek Canyon (the largest Fremont site in Utah)
Nine Mile Canyon (large collection of Fremont rock art)
Edge of the Cedars State Park, Blanding (an Ancestral Puebloan great house)
Hovenweep National Monument and Bears Ears National Monument (Ancestral Puebloan sites)

history.event: Ancestral Puebloan people farm in southern Utah's canyon country, and the Fremont people farm and hunt across much of Utah.
The Goshute, Paiute, Shoshone, Navajo (Diné), and Ute peoples call Utah home. Ute, Shoshone, and Navajo people adopt horses.
The Spanish Domínguez-Escalante expedition travels from Santa Fe as far north as Utah Lake and meets Native people there.

Mexico wins independence from Spain, and the Utah region becomes part of Mexico. In the Mexican period, Mexican, Ute, and Navajo raiders capture Paiute children and sell them into slavery along the Old Spanish Trail.

Brigham Young and the first Mormon pioneers reach the Salt Lake Valley. Three enslaved Black men, Green Flake, Hark Lay, and Oscar Crosby, traveled with the first group. Jane Manning James, a free Black woman, arrives the same year.
The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ends the Mexican-American War, and the Utah region passes from Mexico to the United States.

The territorial legislature passes the Act in Relation to Service, making slavery of Black people legal in Utah Territory, and a second law that allows the enslavement of Native people for up to 20 years.
In the Mountain Meadows massacre, Utah militia members kill about 120 people traveling west in the Baker-Fancher wagon train.
President Abraham Lincoln sets aside the Uintah Valley reservation for Ute people.
Congress bans slavery in all U.S. territories, ending legal slavery in Utah Territory.

The Black Hawk War, the longest and most destructive conflict between settlers and Native peoples in Utah's history, begins in April 1865 near Manti. Ute warriors led by Antonga Black Hawk, joined by some Paiute and Navajo, fight Mormon settlers and militia. Black Hawk makes peace in 1867 and a treaty is signed in 1868, but raids go on until federal troops are sent in 1872.

The first transcontinental railroad is completed with a golden spike at Promontory Summit. An estimated 10,000 to 20,000 Chinese workers built the Central Pacific line, about 10,000 Irish workers built for the Union Pacific, and Black and Mormon workers helped too.

Utah Territory gives women the vote on February 12, and 25 women vote in an election on February 14. Seraph Young is named as the first woman to cast a vote. Women vote for 17 years until a federal law takes the vote away.

trailblazers.name: Green Flake
trailblazers.text: Green Flake was born enslaved in North Carolina and was one of three enslaved Black men in the first Mormon pioneer group to reach the Salt Lake Valley in 1847, where he planted crops and built a house for the Flake family. He gained his freedom between 1850 and 1860, farmed in Union, Utah, and "died a free man."

trailblazers.name: Jane Manning James
trailblazers.text: Jane Elizabeth Manning James was born free, joined the Latter-day Saint church in 1842, and arrived in the Salt Lake Valley in 1847. She gave to temple building funds, spoke up for her right to take part in temple ceremonies, and was honored as one of the original pioneers in 1897.

trailblazers.name: Martha Hughes Cannon
trailblazers.text: Martha Hughes Cannon earned degrees in chemistry, medicine, and pharmacy and worked as a doctor. In 1896 she became the first woman elected to a state senate in the United States, defeating her own husband, and she helped create the Utah State Board of Health.

trailblazers.name: Reva Beck Bosone
trailblazers.text: Reva Beck Bosone was the first woman elected as a judge in Utah and the first woman from Utah elected to the U.S. House, where she served from 1949 to 1953. She backed minimum wage laws for women and children, but she also proposed a law to remove Native nations from federal "wardship"; a version became House Concurrent Resolution 108 in 1953, which was highly contentious.

trailblazers.name: Mae Timbimboo Parry
trailblazers.group: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation woman, historian and advocate
trailblazers.text: Mae Timbimboo Parry was born in Washakie, Utah, and was sent to a boarding school in California at age eight. She recorded the oral histories of her people, changing how people understood the Bear River Massacre, and worked with Congress and the Utah Legislature to protect Native American rights.

trailblazers.name: Kuniko Muramatsu Terasawa
trailblazers.text: Kuniko Terasawa ran the Utah Nippo, a Japanese and English newspaper in Salt Lake City, after her husband died in 1939. She hand-set the type using about 5,000 Japanese characters and kept the paper going through World War II, when it was one of only three such newspapers in America allowed to keep publishing.

trailblazers.name: Mignon Barker Richmond
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, educator and civil rights leader
trailblazers.text: Mignon Barker Richmond was the first Black person to graduate from college in Utah, at Utah State Agricultural College (now Utah State University). She started the state's first school lunch program in 1948, worked with the NAACP, and Richmond Park in Salt Lake City is named for her.

landforms: Kings Peak, the highest point in Utah, in the Uinta Mountains
The Wasatch Fault zone, which stretches from Malad City, Idaho, to Fayette, Utah
Great Basin deserts and valleys in the west
Colorado Plateau red rock canyons in the south and east (Arches, Zion, Capitol Reef)
waters: Great Salt Lake, the shrunken remnant of ancient Lake Bonneville, with no outlet
Wetlands, marshes, and mudflats around the Great Salt Lake
geography.regions: Utah has three main natural regions: the Rocky Mountains, the Great Basin, and the Colorado Plateau.

ecosystems.name: Great Salt Lake
ecosystems.about: The lake is 2 to 7 times saltier than the ocean, yet brine shrimp and brine flies live in it. Up to 12 million migratory birds stop here each year to rest, refuel, and breed, and they depend on the brine shrimp for food.

ecosystems.name: Great Salt Lake wetlands
ecosystems.about: The marshes, mudflats, and meadows around the lake hold the highest concentration of vegetated wetlands in Utah and give birds places to rest and nest.

ecosystems.name: Mountain forests
ecosystems.about: In Utah's mountains, quaking aspen (the state tree) is common, and Rocky Mountain elk (the state animal) live there.

ecosystems.name: Great Basin desert
ecosystems.about: A dry land of valleys and ranges southwest of the Great Salt Lake, where Goshute people gathered pinyon nuts, wild plants and roots, crickets, and grasshoppers for food.

science.weather: Utah is mostly dry, with semi-arid and desert climates, and droughts are becoming more frequent and severe. Hazards include earthquakes along the Wasatch Fault (a magnitude 5.7 quake hit near Magna in March 2020, and scientists estimate a 25 percent chance of a large quake within the next century), flash floods in southern Utah, summer wildfires sparked by dry lightning, lake-effect snow near the Great Salt Lake, and winter inversions that trap air pollution.
science.resources: Utah's economy includes mining, oil, natural gas, coal, salt production (about 2 million tons of salt a year from the Great Salt Lake), brine shrimp harvesting, cattle ranching, technology and research, and tourism.
science.highlight: Dinosaur National Monument: in 1909, paleontologist Earl Douglass found dinosaur bones on the Utah side of the monument. Today the "Wall of Bones" inside the Quarry building shows over 1,500 dinosaur bones from about 150 million years ago, including Allosaurus (Utah's state fossil), Stegosaurus, Apatosaurus, and Diplodocus.

g3_ss.title: Utah's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Salt Lake City and the 29 counties on a map, learn what the Legislature (29 senators, 75 representatives), Governor, and Utah Supreme Court do, and read Article IV, Section 1 about equal rights for women and men.

g3_ss.title: Utah's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Learn that Utah is named for the Ute, compare how the Fremont, Ancestral Puebloans, Goshute, and Ute lived, and meet Utah's eight tribal nations today.

g3_ss.title: Utah Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Make trading cards for Green Flake, Martha Hughes Cannon, Mae Timbimboo Parry, Kuniko Terasawa, and Mignon Barker Richmond, telling what each person did for their community.

g45_ss.title: Utah's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Use a timeline from the first people 12,000 years ago through the Fremont and Ancestral Puebloans to the Ute, Goshute, Paiute, Shoshone, and Diné; study how horses changed life and how reservations and allotments took Ute land.

g45_ss.title: Spanish, Mexican, and Pioneer Utah, 1776–1850
g45_ss.plan: Trace the Domínguez-Escalante route (1776), the Old Spanish Trail and the enslavement of Paiute children, Mexican rule (1821), the 1847 pioneers including Green Flake and Jane Manning James, and the 1848 treaty.

g45_ss.title: Utah Territory to Statehood
g45_ss.plan: Examine the 1852 slavery laws and their end in 1862, the Black Hawk War, the Chinese and Irish workers of the 1869 railroad, women voting in 1870, and statehood in 1896.

g3_sci.title: Life in a Salty Lake
g3_sci.plan: Hatch brine shrimp, test how salt changes floating, and learn why millions of birds stop at the Great Salt Lake.

g3_sci.title: Utah's Dinosaurs
g3_sci.plan: Explore the Wall of Bones at Dinosaur National Monument, compare Allosaurus and Stegosaurus, and make a model fossil.

g3_sci.title: Mountains, Deserts, and Canyons
g3_sci.plan: Sort plants and animals into mountain, desert, and lake habitats, from quaking aspen and elk to pinyon pines and brine shrimp.

g45_sci.title: Lake Bonneville and the Shrinking Great Salt Lake
g45_sci.plan: Map ancient Lake Bonneville, explain why a lake with no outlet becomes salty, and graph how low water raises salinity and dust.

g45_sci.title: Earthquakes on the Wasatch Fault
g45_sci.plan: Model how faults move, study the 2020 Magna earthquake and its aftershocks, and plan an earthquake-safety drill.

g45_sci.title: Reading the Rock Record
g45_sci.plan: Use the 150-million-year-old river rocks at Dinosaur National Monument to learn how fossils form in river deposits and how layers tell time.
